props.title: Overnight

sections.content: Overnight (2003) stands as one of indie film's most brutal cautionary tales. First-time filmmaker Troy Duffy rocketed to fame when Miramax's Harvey Weinstein bought his script for The Boondock Saints (1999) and offered him a deal to direct. The documentary captures Duffy's meteoric rise and catastrophic fall, similar to the industry exposés seen in Lost in La Mancha (2002) and Hearts of Darkness (1991). What makes Overnight particularly compelling is how it documents pure hubris destroying a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

sections.content: The film serves as a masterclass in how not to navigate Hollywood. Where Project Greenlight (2001) showed aspiring filmmakers learning from mistakes, Overnight captures pure self-destruction. Duffy alienates supporters, insults executives, and burns bridges with shocking speed. The documentary crew caught it all, creating an unintentional companion piece to Living in Oblivion (1995) and The Player (1992) - films that dramatized indie filmmaking's pitfalls.

Most compelling is how Overnight contrasts with other Hollywood dream-chase documentaries like Burden of Dreams (1982) and Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker's Apocalypse (1991). Those films show talented directors pushing through adversity. Overnight instead captures a filmmaker creating his own obstacles through arrogance. The result feels like a real-life version of Swimming with Sharks (1994), except the monster isn't a studio executive but the filmmaker himself. SUBHEAD: The Impact on Independent Film

sections.content: The fallout from Overnight rippled through indie film circles. While Swingers (1996) and El Mariachi (1992) inspired filmmakers with their rags-to-riches stories, Overnight became required viewing at film schools as a warning. It's particularly relevant alongside The Kid Stays in the Picture (2002), which shows producer Robert Evans navigating similar industry politics with far more savvy.
